summary.text: A system is in mechanical equilibrium when the net force on each of its parts is zero, so the parts keep a constant momentum and velocity.
Equilibrium can be static, with nothing moving, or it can involve steady motion, like a child sliding down a slide at constant speed.
An equilibrium is stable if a small nudge brings back restoring forces, and unstable if the nudge makes forces push the system farther away.

facts.label: Stable equilibrium
facts.value: Potential energy at a local minimum

facts.label: Unstable equilibrium
facts.value: Potential energy at a local maximum

items.prompt: A child glides down a playground slide at a steady, unchanging speed. How would a physicist describe this?

options.label: Out of equilibrium, since she moves
In static equilibrium, like a paperweight
In mechanical equilibrium, though not at rest
Out of equilibrium, since gravity acts

items.explain: Constant velocity means zero net force, so she is in mechanical equilibrium but not static equilibrium.

items.prompt: A marble rests at the bottom of a bowl and is nudged slightly. What do the forces do?

options.label: Return it toward where it began
Push it farther away
Leave it wherever it was nudged
Make it speed up without limit

items.explain: At a local minimum of potential energy, a small disturbance meets forces that tend to restore equilibrium.

items.prompt: A pencil balanced perfectly on its sharp tip can be in equilibrium, yet it never stays. Why?

options.label: Gravity on it is zero at the tip
Nothing balances it, even undisturbed
Small nudges get absorbed and it settles
Any slight disturbance makes forces carry it farther away

items.explain: At a local maximum of potential energy the equilibrium is unstable, so a tiny displacement grows.

items.prompt: A ball sits on a saddle-shaped surface: nudged sideways it rolls back, nudged forward it rolls off. Is that called stable?

options.label: Yes, since one direction is stable
No, stability needs every direction
Yes, because it started at rest
No, a saddle has no equilibrium

items.explain: Generally an equilibrium is called stable only if it is stable in all directions.

items.prompt: A beam sits on extra supports, and the force and moment balance equations cannot fix every support's push. What can be done?

options.label: Assume the net force is not zero
Drop the equilibrium requirement
Bring in information from outside those equations
Ignore the extra supports

items.explain: Such statically indeterminate cases can often be solved with information beyond the standard equilibrium equations.

items.prompt: Which of these is an object at mechanical equilibrium while at rest?

options.label: A paperweight sitting on a desk
A child sliding at constant speed
A stone dropping faster and faster
A ball speeding down a ramp

items.explain: A paperweight on a desk is the standard example of static equilibrium.
